4. Generating Random Variates

How to turn i.i.d. U(0,1) random numbers into observations from the distributions a model actually needs — the inverse transform and composition methods, and what makes a variate-generation algorithm good.

Goal. Study algorithms that produce observations (realizations) from some desired input distribution, given a stream of i.i.d. U(0,1)U(0,1)U(0,1) random numbers.

Chapter 3 produced the raw material: uniform random numbers. This chapter turns them into random variates from whatever distribution the model calls for — e.g. the exponential interarrival and service times of an M/M/1M/M/1M/M/1 queue.

4.1. Structure

  • It is essential to have a statistically reliable underlying RNG. Every algorithm below assumes its input really is i.i.d. U(0,1)U(0,1)U(0,1); a defective generator corrupts every variate built from it.

Factors in choosing an algorithm.

1. Exactness. An algorithm is exact if the variates it produces have exactly the desired distribution, not merely approximately.

Example of an inexact method. To generate Z∼N(0,1)Z \sim N(0,1)Z∼N(0,1):

  1. Generate u1,…,u12u_1, \dots, u_{12}u1​,…,u12​ i.i.d. U(0,1)U(0,1)U(0,1).
  2. Return Z=u1+u2+⋯+u12−6Z = u_1 + u_2 + \cdots + u_{12} - 6Z=u1​+u2​+⋯+u12​−6.

The moments come out right:

E[Z]=12⋅12−6=0,Var⁡(Z)=12⋅112=1,\mathbf{E}[Z] = 12 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} - 6 = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Z) = 12 \cdot \tfrac{1}{12} = 1, E[Z]=12⋅21​−6=0,Var(Z)=12⋅121​=1,

and by the CLT the sum is approximately normal. But it is not exact. Since each ui∈[0,1]u_i \in [0,1]ui​∈[0,1], the output always satisfies

Z∈[−6,6],Z \in [-6, 6], Z∈[−6,6],

whereas a true N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) variable has range (−∞,∞)(-\infty, \infty)(−∞,∞). The algorithm can never produce a value beyond ±6\pm 6±6, so it truncates both tails — exactly the region that matters most in reliability, risk, and rare-event studies. It is also wasteful: 12 random numbers per variate. Avoid it; use an exact method (§4.2.5) instead.

2. Efficiency.

  • memory usage;
  • execution time, including setup time (some algorithms precompute tables; that cost is paid once but must be counted).

3. Simplicity: easy to understand, implement, and debug. There is a trade-off between efficiency and simplicity — the fastest algorithm is rarely the clearest.

4. If possible, use exactly one random number per random variate. Reasons:

  • Simplicity.
  • Synchronization. When comparing two systems with common random numbers (§3.3, practical issue 3), we want the iii-th variate in system A to be built from the same uiu_iui​ as in system B. If one system consumes a variable number of uniforms per variate, the two streams drift out of step and the comparison loses its sharpness.
  • Monotonicity. With one uniform per variate and X=F−1(u)X = F^{-1}(u)X=F−1(u), the variate is a monotone function of uuu. This is what makes variance-reduction techniques such as antithetic variates work.

4.2. RVG Algorithms

Direct methods — build the variate straight from the definition of the distribution:

  1. Inverse transform — universally applicable in principle, but may be hard to implement.
  2. Composition ⎫
  3. Convolution ⎭ — apply only to input distributions of a specific form (mixtures and sums, respectively).

When these fail — that is, when F−1F^{-1}F−1 has no usable closed form and the distribution is neither a convenient mixture nor a convenient sum (the normal, gamma, and beta distributions are the standard examples) — fall back on:

  1. Acceptance–rejection method.
  2. Special techniques, e.g. for normal random variables.

4.2.1. Inverse Transform Method

Continuous case. Let XXX be a continuous r.v. with c.d.f. FFF.

Algorithm.

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=F−1(u)X = F^{-1}(u)X=F−1(u).

The catch is step 2: F−1F^{-1}F−1 must be computed, and for many distributions (normal, gamma, beta) it has no closed form.

Proof that the output has c.d.f. FFF.

P(X≤x)=P(F−1(u)≤x)=P(F(F−1(u))≤F(x))applying F to both sides; valid since F is non-decreasing=P(u≤F(x))=F(x)since u∼U(0,1).\begin{aligned} P(X \le x) &= P\left(F^{-1}(u) \le x\right) \\ &= P\left(F(F^{-1}(u)) \le F(x)\right) && \text{applying } F \text{ to both sides; valid since } F \text{ is non-decreasing} \\ &= P\left(u \le F(x)\right) \\ &= F(x) && \text{since } u \sim U(0,1). \end{aligned} P(X≤x)​=P(F−1(u)≤x)=P(F(F−1(u))≤F(x))=P(u≤F(x))=F(x)​​applying F to both sides; valid since F is non-decreasingsince u∼U(0,1).​

The last step is the definition of the uniform distribution: P(u≤a)=aP(u \le a) = aP(u≤a)=a for any a∈[0,1]a \in [0,1]a∈[0,1], and here a=F(x)a = F(x)a=F(x) is indeed in [0,1][0,1][0,1] because it is a probability. So the c.d.f. of the generated XXX is FFF, exactly — the method is exact.

Example: X∼Exp(λ)X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)X∼Exp(λ). Here F(x)=1−e−λxF(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}F(x)=1−e−λx for x>0x > 0x>0. Set u=F(x)u = F(x)u=F(x) and solve:

u=1−e−λx  ⟹  e−λx=1−u  ⟹  x=−1λln⁡(1−u).u = 1 - e^{-\lambda x} \;\Longrightarrow\; e^{-\lambda x} = 1 - u \;\Longrightarrow\; x = -\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1 - u). u=1−e−λx⟹e−λx=1−u⟹x=−λ1​ln(1−u).

Algorithm.

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=−1λln⁡(1−u)X = -\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1-u)X=−λ1​ln(1−u).

Variant. Replace step 2 by “2′. Return X=−1λln⁡uX = -\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln uX=−λ1​lnu.”

This is valid because 1−u∼U(0,1)1 - u \sim U(0,1)1−u∼U(0,1) whenever u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1), so the two versions produce the same distribution. It saves one subtraction per variate — a genuine but small gain in a tight loop.

Two cautions, though:

  • Monotonicity is lost. Version 2 is increasing in uuu; version 2′ is decreasing. Under 2, a large uuu gives a long interarrival time in both of two systems being compared; under 2′ the correspondence is reversed. Where synchronization or antithetic variates matter, prefer 2.
  • The value u=0u = 0u=0. An LCG can output u=0u = 0u=0 (when zi=0z_i = 0zi​=0), and ln⁡0\ln 0ln0 is undefined. Version 2 never has this problem, since 1−u∈(0,1]1 - u \in (0, 1]1−u∈(0,1]. If 2′ is used, u=0u = 0u=0 must be screened out.

Efficiency problem. The number of comparisons the chain performs equals III, the index it returns. Since the algorithm returns xix_ixi​ exactly when I=iI = iI=i, and P(I=i)=P(X=xi)=p(xi)P(I = i) = P(X = x_i) = p(x_i)P(I=i)=P(X=xi​)=p(xi​), the number of comparisons NNN is a random variable with the same distribution as the index, so by the definition of expectation,

E[N]=∑i=1ni⋅P(N=i)=∑i=1ni p(xi).\mathbf{E}[N] = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot P(N = i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i\, p(x_i). E[N]=i=1∑n​i⋅P(N=i)=i=1∑n​ip(xi​).

If the probable values sit late in the list, this is close to nnn: tiny jumps at x1,x2,…x_1, x_2, \dotsx1​,x2​,… and the big jumps only at the end.

Two fixes.

  1. Binary search. Since F(x1)≤F(x2)≤⋯≤F(xn)F(x_1) \le F(x_2) \le \cdots \le F(x_n)F(x1​)≤F(x2​)≤⋯≤F(xn​) is a sorted array, locate uuu by bisection instead of scanning: O(log⁡2n)O(\log_2 n)O(log2​n) comparisons instead of O(n)O(n)O(n), whatever the probabilities.

  2. Reorder the comparisons. Test the values in decreasing order of probability. Relabel so that p(1)≥p(2)≥⋯≥p(n)p_{(1)} \ge p_{(2)} \ge \cdots \ge p_{(n)}p(1)​≥p(2)​≥⋯≥p(n)​ and build the cumulative sums for that new order; then E[N]=∑ii p(i)\mathbf{E}[N] = \sum_i i\, p_{(i)}E[N]=∑i​ip(i)​ is as small as possible. The reordering is done once in setup, so it costs nothing at run time.

Example. n=6n = 6n=6 with p=(0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50)p = (0.05,\, 0.05,\, 0.10,\, 0.10,\, 0.20,\, 0.50)p=(0.05,0.05,0.10,0.10,0.20,0.50):

order of testing E[comparisons]\mathbf{E}[\text{comparisons}]E[comparisons]
as given: x1,x2,…,x6x_1, x_2, \dots, x_6x1​,x2​,…,x6​ ∑ii pi=4.85\sum_i i\,p_i = 4.85∑i​ipi​=4.85
decreasing probability: x6,x5,x3,x4,x1,x2x_6, x_5, x_3, x_4, x_1, x_2x6​,x5​,x3​,x4​,x1​,x2​ ∑ii p(i)=2.15\sum_i i\,p_{(i)} = 2.15∑i​ip(i)​=2.15

More than twice as fast, for no cost beyond sorting once.

Does reordering change the simulation? No. The output distribution is exactly the same — each xix_ixi​ is still returned with probability p(xi)p(x_i)p(xi​), because the intervals of (0,1](0,1](0,1] assigned to the values have the same widths p(xi)p(x_i)p(xi​); only their positions along (0,1](0,1](0,1] are permuted. The only thing that changes is the expected number of comparisons, i.e. the run time.

The one side effect: reordering destroys the monotone relationship between uuu and XXX, so the output is no longer F−1(u)F^{-1}(u)F−1(u) as a function of uuu. If synchronization or antithetic variates matter (see “Advantages” below), keep the natural order or use binary search, which preserves it.

Example: discrete uniform. X∼DU(1,100)X \sim DU(1,100)X∼DU(1,100), i.e. X∈{1,2,…,100}X \in \{1, 2, \dots, 100\}X∈{1,2,…,100} with p(i)=1100p(i) = \frac{1}{100}p(i)=1001​ for every iii, so F(i)=i100F(i) = \frac{i}{100}F(i)=100i​.

The general algorithm becomes:

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. if u ≤ 0.01 return X = 1; else if u ≤ 0.02 return X = 2; … ; else return X = 100

But here the chain can be replaced by a formula. The first iii with u≤i/100u \le i/100u≤i/100 is characterized by

i−1100<u≤i100⟺i−1<100u≤i⟺i=⌈100u⌉,\frac{i-1}{100} < u \le \frac{i}{100} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i - 1 < 100u \le i \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i = \lceil 100u \rceil, 100i−1​<u≤100i​⟺i−1<100u≤i⟺i=⌈100u⌉,

so step 2 collapses to

  X=⌈100u⌉  \boxed{\;X = \lceil 100 u \rceil\;} X=⌈100u⌉​

— one multiplication and one ceiling, instead of up to 100 comparisons. (Equal probabilities are what make this possible; unequal ones need the search.)

Generalized inverse transform. To cover continuous, discrete, and mixed distributions in one statement:

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=min⁡{x:F(x)≥u}X = \min\{x : F(x) \ge u\}X=min{x:F(x)≥u}.

This is the same rule as before, written so it always makes sense. An ordinary inverse F−1F^{-1}F−1 requires FFF to be strictly increasing and continuous; a discrete FFF is flat in places (so no unique inverse) and jumps in places (so some values of uuu have no xxx with F(x)=uF(x) = uF(x)=u at all). Taking the smallest xxx whose F(x)F(x)F(x) has reached uuu handles both defects, and reduces to the usual F−1(u)F^{-1}(u)F−1(u) when FFF is continuous and strictly increasing.

Advantages and disadvantages of the inverse transform method.

Disadvantages.

  1. Must invert the c.d.f., which may have no closed form (normal, gamma, beta).
  2. May not be the most efficient approach even when the inverse exists.

Advantages.

  1. Easy to generate from truncated distributions. Truncating means restricting XXX to an interval [a,b][a,b][a,b] and renormalizing:

    F∗(x)=F(x)−F(a)F(b)−F(a),a≤x≤b,F^*(x) = \frac{F(x) - F(a)}{F(b) - F(a)}, \qquad a \le x \le b, F∗(x)=F(b)−F(a)F(x)−F(a)​,a≤x≤b,

    which is the original density chopped off outside [a,b][a,b][a,b] and scaled up so the area is again 1.

    Inverting F∗F^*F∗ costs nothing extra: generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1) and return

    X=F−1(F(a)+u [F(b)−F(a)]).X = F^{-1}\Big(F(a) + u\,\big[F(b) - F(a)\big]\Big). X=F−1(F(a)+u[F(b)−F(a)]).

    In words: instead of drawing uuu uniformly over all of (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), draw it uniformly over the slice (F(a),F(b))\big(F(a), F(b)\big)(F(a),F(b)) of the vertical axis. Every draw is usable — no rejection, one uniform per variate.

  2. Facilitates variance reduction when comparing alternative systems. Let X1∼F1X_1 \sim F_1X1​∼F1​ be the output of system 1 and X2∼F2X_2 \sim F_2X2​∼F2​ that of system 2, and suppose we want the difference in mean cost,

    E[X1]−E[X2]=E[X1−X2],\mathbf{E}[X_1] - \mathbf{E}[X_2] = \mathbf{E}[X_1 - X_2], E[X1​]−E[X2​]=E[X1​−X2​],

    so that X1−X2X_1 - X_2X1​−X2​ is an unbiased estimator of the gap. Generate both by inverse transform, X1=F1−1(u1)X_1 = F_1^{-1}(u_1)X1​=F1−1​(u1​) and X2=F2−1(u2)X_2 = F_2^{-1}(u_2)X2​=F2−1​(u2​). Since

    Var⁡(X1−X2)=Var⁡(X1)+Var⁡(X2)−2cov⁡(X1,X2),\operatorname{Var}(X_1 - X_2) = \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{Var}(X_2) - 2\operatorname{cov}(X_1, X_2), Var(X1​−X2​)=Var(X1​)+Var(X2​)−2cov(X1​,X2​),

    the precision of the comparison is controlled entirely by how we couple u1u_1u1​ and u2u_2u2​:

coupling cov⁡(X1,X2)\operatorname{cov}(X_1, X_2)cov(X1​,X2​) Var⁡(X1−X2)\operatorname{Var}(X_1 - X_2)Var(X1​−X2​)
1. u1⊥u2u_1 \perp u_2u1​⊥u2​ (independent) 000 Var⁡(X1)+Var⁡(X2)\operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{Var}(X_2)Var(X1​)+Var(X2​)
2. u1=u2u_1 = u_2u1​=u2​ (common random numbers) >0> 0>0 smaller
3. u1=1−u2u_1 = 1 - u_2u1​=1−u2​ (antithetic) <0< 0<0 larger

Case 2 is the useful one. Both F1−1F_1^{-1}F1−1​ and F2−1F_2^{-1}F2−1​ are non-decreasing, so a large uuu pushes both X1X_1X1​ and X2X_2X2​ up and a small uuu pushes both down: the two outputs move together, cov⁡(X1,X2)>0\operatorname{cov}(X_1,X_2) > 0cov(X1​,X2​)>0, and the variance of the difference drops. Note X1≠X2X_1 \ne X_2X1​=X2​ still, since F1≠F2F_1 \ne F_2F1​=F2​. Monotonicity is exactly what the inverse transform provides and what a rejection-based method does not — hence “facilitates”.

(Case 3 is not useless in general; antithetic variates reduce variance when estimating a single mean by averaging X1X_1X1​ and X2X_2X2​, where the negative correlation helps. It is only harmful here, where we take a difference.)

4.2.2. Composition

The name. The target distribution is composed of simpler ones — the way a mixture’s chemical composition lists its ingredients. The method is also called the mixture method: decompose FFF into pieces you know how to sample from, pick a piece at random, then sample from it.

Setup. Use this when FFF can be written as a convex combination of other c.d.f.s F1,F2,…F_1, F_2, \dotsF1​,F2​,… (finitely or infinitely many):

F(x)=∑j≥1pjFj(x),∑j≥1pj=1,pj≥0.F(x) = \sum_{j \ge 1} p_j F_j(x), \qquad \sum_{j \ge 1} p_j = 1, \quad p_j \ge 0 . F(x)=j≥1∑​pj​Fj​(x),j≥1∑​pj​=1,pj​≥0.

Equivalently, in terms of densities or mass functions,

f(x)=∑j≥1pjfj(x)orp(x)=∑j≥1pj p(j)(x).f(x) = \sum_{j \ge 1} p_j f_j(x) \qquad\text{or}\qquad p(x) = \sum_{j \ge 1} p_j\, p^{(j)}(x). f(x)=j≥1∑​pj​fj​(x)orp(x)=j≥1∑​pj​p(j)(x).

Algorithm.

  1. Generate a positive random integer JJJ with P(J=j)=pjP(J = j) = p_jP(J=j)=pj​ (a discrete variate — use the inverse transform of §4.2.1).
  2. Return XXX generated from the c.d.f. FJF_JFJ​.

Proof. Conditioning on JJJ,

P(X≤x)=∑j≥1P(X≤x∣J=j) P(J=j)=∑j≥1Fj(x) pj=F(x).■P(X \le x) = \sum_{j \ge 1} P(X \le x \mid J = j)\, P(J = j) = \sum_{j \ge 1} F_j(x)\, p_j = F(x). \qquad \blacksquare P(X≤x)=j≥1∑​P(X≤x∣J=j)P(J=j)=j≥1∑​Fj​(x)pj​=F(x).■

f(x)={a+2(1−a)x,0≤x≤1(0<a<1),0,otherwise.f(x) = \begin{cases} a + 2(1-a)x, & 0 \le x \le 1 \quad (0 < a < 1), \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} f(x)={a+2(1−a)x,0,​0≤x≤1(0<a<1),otherwise.​

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).

Efficiency comparison (expected operations per variate):

uuu’s comparisons additions multiplications square roots
inverse 1 1 1.5 1 1
composition 2 1 1.5 0 1

How the counts are obtained. Each row averages the two branches, which are taken with probability 12\tfrac1221​ each; a subtraction counts as an addition. For the inverse method, the left branch −1+2u-1 + \sqrt{2u}−1+2u​ uses one multiplication (2u2u2u), one square root and one addition, while the right branch 1−2(1−u)1 - \sqrt{2(1-u)}1−2(1−u)​ uses one multiplication (2×2 \times2×), one square root and two additions (1−u1-u1−u and 1−⋅1 - \sqrt{\cdot}1−⋅​) — so the average is 12(1)+12(2)=1.5\tfrac12(1) + \tfrac12(2) = 1.521​(1)+21​(2)=1.5 additions, with 1 multiplication and 1 square root either way, plus the single comparison u<12u < \tfrac12u<21​ and the single uniform. For composition, u2−1\sqrt{u_2} - 1u2​​−1 has one addition and 1−1−u21 - \sqrt{1-u_2}1−1−u2​​ has two, giving the same 1.51.51.5 average and the same one square root and one comparison, but no multiplication — the factor 2 never appears, because doubling the density was absorbed into choosing a half. The cost is that u1u_1u1​ is spent on the coin toss and u2u_2u2​ on the value, so two uniforms are consumed instead of one.

Conclusion. The two methods differ in exactly two places: composition saves one multiplication but spends one extra random number. Generating a random number is far more expensive than a multiplication, so the inverse transform is more efficient here. (It also keeps XXX monotone in uuu, which composition does not — see §4.2.1, advantage 4.)

4.2.3. Convolution

Setup. Let Y1,Y2,…,YmY_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_mY1​,Y2​,…,Ym​ be i.i.d. with common c.d.f. GGG, and define

X=Y1+Y2+⋯+Ym.X = Y_1 + Y_2 + \cdots + Y_m . X=Y1​+Y2​+⋯+Ym​.

The c.d.f. FFF of XXX is called the mmm-fold convolution of GGG with itself. Use this method whenever the target distribution is known to arise as such a sum.

Algorithm (to generate from FFF):

  1. Generate Y1,…,YmY_1, \dots, Y_mY1​,…,Ym​ independently from GGG.

Why the proof is trivial. Unlike the inverse transform or composition, there is nothing to verify: FFF was defined as the distribution of the sum, and the algorithm literally forms that sum from independent draws. Correctness is by construction. The work in this method lies elsewhere — in recognizing that the desired FFF is a convolution of something samplable.

So “waiting for the nnn-th event” and “counting events” are two views of the same process.

  1. Generate Y1,…,YnY_1, \dots, Y_nY1​,…,Yn​ i.i.d. Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ) (each by inverse transform, §4.2.1).

This is exact and trivially correct, but it costs nnn uniforms and nnn logarithms per variate. One improvement is free:

X=∑i=1n(−1λln⁡ui)=−1λln⁡ ⁣(∏i=1nui),X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln u_i\right) = -\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} u_i\right), X=i=1∑n​(−λ1​lnui​)=−λ1​ln(i=1∏n​ui​),

Composition vs. convolution. Both write the target in terms of simpler distributions, but in opposite ways:

Differentiating gives the density of ZZZ:

fZ(z)=FZ′(z)={z,0≤z≤1,−z+2,1≤z≤2,f_Z(z) = F_Z'(z) = \begin{cases} z, & 0 \le z \le 1, \\ -z + 2, & 1 \le z \le 2, \end{cases} fZ​(z)=FZ′​(z)={z,−z+2,​0≤z≤1,1≤z≤2,​

a triangle on [0,2][0, 2][0,2] with peak at z=1z = 1z=1. Subtracting 1 slides it to [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]: X=Z−1X = Z - 1X=Z−1 has fX(x)=fZ(x+1)f_X(x) = f_Z(x + 1)fX​(x)=fZ​(x+1), which is x+1x + 1x+1 on [−1,0][-1, 0][−1,0] and −(x+1)+2=1−x-(x+1) + 2 = 1 - x−(x+1)+2=1−x on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] — exactly the target.

Algorithm (convolution).

  1. Generate u1⊥u2∼U(0,1)u_1 \perp u_2 \sim U(0,1)u1​⊥u2​∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=u1+u2−1X = u_1 + u_2 - 1X=u1​+u2​−1.

Why this beats both earlier methods. Add the new row to the table from §4.2.2:

uuu’s comparisons additions multiplications square roots
inverse 1 1 1.5 1 1
composition 2 1 1.5 0 1
convolution 2 0 2 0 0

Convolution uses the same two uniforms as composition but eliminates the comparison, the multiplication, and above all the square root, at the price of half an extra addition. A square root is by far the most expensive operation in the table — many times the cost of an addition, and more than the cost of drawing a uniform — so removing it outweighs the second uniform, and convolution is the most efficient of the three for this distribution. (Against inverse transform, the trade is one extra uniform plus half an addition in exchange for dropping a comparison, a multiplication and a square root; the square root alone settles it.)

4.2.4. Acceptance–Rejection (AR)

Where it sits. Methods 1–3 (§4.2.1–4.2.3) are direct: they compute XXX from the uniforms by a formula. Acceptance–rejection is the indirect method from the list in §4.2: it does not compute XXX; it generates candidates from an easier distribution and keeps only some of them. The arrow in the lecture outline (“rejection → indirect”) just records that classification.

When to use it. When the desired p.d.f. fff has a form too complex to invert or decompose.

Idea. Use a simple, easy-to-sample p.d.f. — a surrogate — that approximates fff from above, then correct for the difference by discarding a fraction of the draws.

Setup. Choose a majorizing function ttt with

t(x)≥f(x)for all x.t(x) \ge f(x) \quad \text{for all } x . t(x)≥f(x)for all x.

Then

c=∫−∞∞t(x) dx  ≥  ∫−∞∞f(x) dx=1,c = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} t(x)\,dx \;\ge\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1, c=∫−∞∞​t(x)dx≥∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=1,

so ttt is not a density (its area exceeds 1), but its normalization

r(x)=t(x)cr(x) = \frac{t(x)}{c} r(x)=ct(x)​

is a valid p.d.f. (r≥0r \ge 0r≥0 and ∫r=c/c=1\int r = c/c = 1∫r=c/c=1). rrr is the surrogate we actually sample from.

AR algorithm.

  1. Generate Y∼rY \sim rY∼r.
  2. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1), independent of YYY.
  3. If u≤f(Y)t(Y)u \le \dfrac{f(Y)}{t(Y)}u≤t(Y)f(Y)​, return X=YX = YX=Y (accept).
  4. Otherwise discard YYY and go back to step 1.

On step 1: YYY is generated from the surrogate rrr, not from fff — that is the whole point. Since rrr was chosen to be simple, this is done by one of the direct methods (typically inverse transform). YYY is only a candidate for XXX; steps 3–4 decide whether it becomes one.

On step 3: the ratio f(Y)/t(Y)f(Y)/t(Y)f(Y)/t(Y) lies in [0,1][0,1][0,1] because t≥ft \ge ft≥f. Comparing it with a uniform means: accept YYY with probability f(Y)/t(Y)f(Y)/t(Y)f(Y)/t(Y). Where ttt hugs fff this is near 1 (almost always accept); where ttt is far above fff it is small (usually reject). The rejections thin out exactly the regions where rrr over-samples relative to fff.

Proof that the output has c.d.f. FFF. The returned XXX is a candidate YYY given that it was accepted, so

P(X≤x)=P(Y≤x∣Y accepted)=P(Y≤x,  Y accepted)P(Y accepted).P(X \le x) = P(Y \le x \mid Y \text{ accepted}) = \frac{P(Y \le x,\; Y \text{ accepted})}{P(Y \text{ accepted})} . P(X≤x)=P(Y≤x∣Y accepted)=P(Y accepted)P(Y≤x,Y accepted)​.

We compute the denominator first (it is also the efficiency, comment 2 below):

P(Y accepted)=P ⁣(u≤f(Y)t(Y))=∫−∞∞P ⁣(u≤f(Y)t(Y)  |  Y=y)r(y) dy(condition on Y)=∫−∞∞P ⁣(u≤f(y)t(y))r(y) dy(u⊥Y, so the condition drops)=∫−∞∞f(y)t(y)⋅t(y)c dy(P(u≤a)=a;  r=t/c)=1c∫−∞∞f(y) dy=1c.\begin{aligned} P(Y \text{ accepted}) &= P\!\left(u \le \tfrac{f(Y)}{t(Y)}\right) \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} P\!\left(u \le \tfrac{f(Y)}{t(Y)} \;\middle|\; Y = y\right) r(y)\,dy && \text{(condition on } Y\text{)} \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} P\!\left(u \le \tfrac{f(y)}{t(y)}\right) r(y)\,dy && (u \perp Y \text{, so the condition drops}) \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(y)}{t(y)} \cdot \frac{t(y)}{c}\,dy && (P(u \le a) = a;\; r = t/c) \\ &= \frac{1}{c}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y)\,dy = \frac{1}{c} . \end{aligned} P(Y accepted)​=P(u≤t(Y)f(Y)​)=∫−∞∞​P(u≤t(Y)f(Y)​​Y=y)r(y)dy=∫−∞∞​P(u≤t(y)f(y)​)r(y)dy=∫−∞∞​t(y)f(y)​⋅ct(y)​dy=c1​∫−∞∞​f(y)dy=c1​.​​(condition on Y)(u⊥Y, so the condition drops)(P(u≤a)=a;r=t/c)​

The numerator is the same calculation with the extra event Y≤xY \le xY≤x, which after conditioning on Y=yY = yY=y just restricts the integral to y≤xy \le xy≤x:

P(Y≤x,  Y accepted)=∫−∞xf(y)t(y)⋅t(y)c dy=1c∫−∞xf(y) dy=F(x)c.P(Y \le x,\; Y \text{ accepted}) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} \frac{f(y)}{t(y)} \cdot \frac{t(y)}{c}\,dy = \frac{1}{c}\int_{-\infty}^{x} f(y)\,dy = \frac{F(x)}{c} . P(Y≤x,Y accepted)=∫−∞x​t(y)f(y)​⋅ct(y)​dy=c1​∫−∞x​f(y)dy=cF(x)​.

Dividing,

P(X≤x)=F(x)/c1/c=F(x).■P(X \le x) = \frac{F(x)/c}{1/c} = F(x). \qquad\blacksquare P(X≤x)=1/cF(x)/c​=F(x).■

Note the mechanism: t(y)t(y)t(y) cancels between the acceptance probability f/tf/tf/t and the surrogate density t/ct/ct/c, and ccc cancels between numerator and denominator. Whatever shape ttt has, the output is exactly fff — the choice of ttt affects only speed, never correctness.

Comments.

  1. Generating from rrr must be much easier than generating from fff; otherwise there is no point in using a surrogate. In practice, choose simple majorizing functions — piecewise constant or piecewise linear.

  2. The algorithm loops until a pair (u,Y)(u, Y)(u,Y) with u≤f(Y)/t(Y)u \le f(Y)/t(Y)u≤f(Y)/t(Y) turns up. From the proof,

    P(Y accepted)=1c=1area under t,P(reject)=1−1c.P(Y \text{ accepted}) = \frac{1}{c} = \frac{1}{\text{area under } t}, \qquad P(\text{reject}) = 1 - \frac{1}{c}. P(Y accepted)=c1​=area under t1​,P(reject)=1−c1​.

    Why the average number of trials is ccc: each pass through steps 1–3 is an independent trial with success probability p=1/cp = 1/cp=1/c (fresh YYY and uuu each time). The number of trials until the first success is therefore Geometric(p)(p)(p), whose mean is 1/p=c1/p = c1/p=c. So ccc uniforms-pairs are consumed per variate on average — a large ccc means a slow generator.

  3. P(Y accepted)=1/cP(Y \text{ accepted}) = 1/cP(Y accepted)=1/c is called the efficiency of the AR method. We want it as close to 1 as possible, i.e. ttt as tight around fff as possible — but a tighter ttt is usually a more complicated one, harder to sample from. This is the same simplicity vs. efficiency trade-off as in §4.1.

Example. f(x)=32x2f(x) = \frac{3}{2}x^2f(x)=23​x2 on (−1,1)(-1, 1)(−1,1) (and 000 elsewhere). Check: ∫−1132x2 dx=1\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{3}{2}x^2\,dx = 1∫−11​23​x2dx=1. The maximum of fff is 32\frac3223​, at x=±1x = \pm 1x=±1.

First attempt: a flat majorizing function. Take t(x)=32t(x) = \frac{3}{2}t(x)=23​ on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) — the smallest constant that stays above fff. Then c=32⋅2=3c = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 2 = 3c=23​⋅2=3 and r(x)=t(x)/3=12r(x) = t(x)/3 = \frac{1}{2}r(x)=t(x)/3=21​ on (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1), i.e. rrr is the U(−1,1)U(-1,1)U(−1,1) density.

  1. Generate Y∼U(−1,1)Y \sim U(-1, 1)Y∼U(−1,1) (e.g. Y=2u′−1Y = 2u' - 1Y=2u′−1 with u′∼U(0,1)u' \sim U(0,1)u′∼U(0,1)).
  2. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1), independent of YYY.
  3. If u≤Y2u \le Y^2u≤Y2, return X=YX = YX=Y.   (f(Y)t(Y)=32Y232=Y2)\;\left(\dfrac{f(Y)}{t(Y)} = \dfrac{\frac32 Y^2}{\frac32} = Y^2\right)(t(Y)f(Y)​=23​23​Y2​=Y2)

Efficiency =1/c=1/3= 1/c = 1/3=1/c=1/3: on average three candidates (six uniforms) per accepted variate. The waste is visible in the figure — the rectangle under ttt has area 3 while the bowl under fff has area 1, and everything in between is rejected.

4.2.5. Special Techniques

There is no general recipe here. A special technique exploits some property that the target distribution happens to have — a relation to another distribution we already know how to sample. Two small examples now; the big one (the normal distribution) gets its own treatment in §4.3.

Example: chi-square with one degree of freedom. Recall from §2.6.3 that if Y∼N(0,1)Y \sim N(0,1)Y∼N(0,1) then Y2∼χ12Y^2 \sim \chi^2_1Y2∼χ12​. So:

  1. Generate Y∼N(0,1)Y \sim N(0,1)Y∼N(0,1) (§4.3).
  2. Return X=Y2X = Y^2X=Y2.

Combining with convolution: χk2\chi^2_kχk2​ is the sum of kkk independent χ12\chi^2_1χ12​ variables, so X=Y12+⋯+Yk2X = Y_1^2 + \cdots + Y_k^2X=Y12​+⋯+Yk2​ with YiY_iYi​ i.i.d. N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1).

Example: geometric by Bernoulli trials. Let X∼Geo(p)X \sim \text{Geo}(p)X∼Geo(p) be the number of trials needed until the first success, each trial succeeding with probability ppp. Simulate the trials literally:

  1. Set X=1X = 1X=1.
  2. Generate Y∼Bernoulli(p)Y \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)Y∼Bernoulli(p) (i.e. u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1) and Y=1Y = 1Y=1 if u≤pu \le pu≤p).
  3. If Y=1Y = 1Y=1, return XXX.
  4. Otherwise set X=X+1X = X + 1X=X+1 and go back to step 2.

This is exact and transparent, but it consumes one uniform per trial, and the expected number of trials is E[X]=1/p\mathbf{E}[X] = 1/pE[X]=1/p. For p=0.01p = 0.01p=0.01 that is 100 uniforms per variate. §4.4 gives a one-uniform formula instead.

4.3. Generating Continuous Random Variates

§4.2 presented the methods abstractly. This section collects the concrete algorithms actually used for the common continuous distributions.

Uniform U(a,b)U(a,b)U(a,b). Inverse transform: F(x)=x−ab−aF(x) = \frac{x-a}{b-a}F(x)=b−ax−a​ on [a,b][a,b][a,b], so u=x−ab−a  ⟺  x=a+(b−a)uu = \frac{x-a}{b-a} \iff x = a + (b-a)uu=b−ax−a​⟺x=a+(b−a)u.

  2. Return X=a+(b−a) uX = a + (b-a)\,uX=a+(b−a)u.

Exponential Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ). From §4.2.1:

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=−1λln⁡uX = -\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln uX=−λ1​lnu.

Erlang(m,λ)(m, \lambda)(m,λ). From §4.2.3, X=Y1+⋯+YmX = Y_1 + \cdots + Y_mX=Y1​+⋯+Ym​ with YiY_iYi​ i.i.d. Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ):

  1. Generate u1,…,um∼U(0,1)u_1, \dots, u_m \sim U(0,1)u1​,…,um​∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=−1λln⁡ ⁣(∏i=1mui)X = -\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m u_i\right)X=−λ1​ln(∏i=1m​ui​).

(Gamma with non-integer shape, Weibull, beta, etc. need special-purpose methods, mostly acceptance–rejection; not covered here.)

4.3.1. Normal distribution: the Box–Muller method

The normal c.d.f. has no closed-form inverse, so inverse transform is out. Composition and convolution do not apply. The trick is a special technique: look at two independent standard normals at once and switch to polar coordinates.

The key fact. Let X1⊥X2∼N(0,1)X_1 \perp X_2 \sim N(0,1)X1​⊥X2​∼N(0,1) and write the point (X1,X2)(X_1, X_2)(X1​,X2​) in polar form:

R2=X12+X22,Θ=tan⁡−1 ⁣(X2X1).R^2 = X_1^2 + X_2^2, \qquad \Theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{X_2}{X_1}\right). R2=X12​+X22​,Θ=tan−1(X1​X2​​).

Then R2R^2R2 and Θ\ThetaΘ are independent, with

R2∼Exp ⁣(12) (rate 12, mean 2),Θ∼U(0,2π).R^2 \sim \text{Exp}\!\left(\tfrac12\right) \ \text{(rate } \tfrac12\text{, mean } 2), \qquad \Theta \sim U(0, 2\pi). R2∼Exp(21​) (rate 21​, mean 2),Θ∼U(0,2π).

Why. The joint density of (X1,X2)(X_1, X_2)(X1​,X2​) is the product of two N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) densities:

fX1,X2(x1,x2)=12πe−x12/2⋅12πe−x22/2=12πexp⁡ ⁣(−x12+x222).f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x_1^2/2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x_2^2/2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x_1^2 + x_2^2}{2}\right). fX1​,X2​​(x1​,x2​)=2π​1​e−x12​/2⋅2π​1​e−x22​/2=2π1​exp(−2x12​+x22​​).

It depends on (x1,x2)(x_1, x_2)(x1​,x2​) only through x12+x22=r2x_1^2 + x_2^2 = r^2x12​+x22​=r2 — the density is rotationally symmetric, which is why the angle will come out uniform. To change variables to (S,Θ)=(R2,Θ)(S, \Theta) = (R^2, \Theta)(S,Θ)=(R2,Θ) we need the Jacobian of the map g1(x1,x2)=x12+x22g_1(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2g1​(x1​,x2​)=x12​+x22​, g2(x1,x2)=tan⁡−1(x2/x1)g_2(x_1,x_2) = \tan^{-1}(x_2/x_1)g2​(x1​,x2​)=tan−1(x2​/x1​). Using ddxtan⁡−1x=11+x2\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}dxd​tan−1x=1+x21​,

J=∣∂g1/∂x1∂g1/∂x2∂g2/∂x1∂g2/∂x2∣=∣2x12x2−x2x12+x22x1x12+x22∣=2x12+2x22x12+x22=2.J = \begin{vmatrix} \partial g_1/\partial x_1 & \partial g_1/\partial x_2 \\ \partial g_2/\partial x_1 & \partial g_2/\partial x_2 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 2x_1 & 2x_2 \\ -\dfrac{x_2}{x_1^2+x_2^2} & \dfrac{x_1}{x_1^2+x_2^2} \end{vmatrix} = \frac{2x_1^2 + 2x_2^2}{x_1^2 + x_2^2} = 2 . J=​∂g1​/∂x1​∂g2​/∂x1​​∂g1​/∂x2​∂g2​/∂x2​​​=​2x1​−x12​+x22​x2​​​2x2​x12​+x22​x1​​​​=x12​+x22​2x12​+2x22​​=2.

The change-of-variables formula gives fS,Θ(s,θ)=fX1,X2(x1,x2) ∣J∣−1f_{S,\Theta}(s,\theta) = f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)\,|J|^{-1}fS,Θ​(s,θ)=fX1​,X2​​(x1​,x2​)∣J∣−1, so

fS,Θ(s,θ)=12πe−s/2⋅12=12e−s/2⏟Exp(1/2) density in s  ⋅  12π⏟U(0,2π) density in θ,s≥0, 0≤θ<2π.f_{S,\Theta}(s, \theta) = \frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-s/2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-s/2}}_{\text{Exp}(1/2)\text{ density in } s}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2\pi}}_{U(0,2\pi)\text{ density in }\theta}, \qquad s \ge 0,\ 0 \le \theta < 2\pi . fS,Θ​(s,θ)=2π1​e−s/2⋅21​=Exp(1/2) density in s21​e−s/2​​⋅U(0,2π) density in θ2π1​​​,s≥0, 0≤θ<2π.

The joint density factors into a function of sss alone times a function of θ\thetaθ alone, which is exactly the statement that S=R2S = R^2S=R2 and Θ\ThetaΘ are independent with those marginals.

Run it backwards. We know how to generate both pieces: R2∼Exp(12)R^2 \sim \text{Exp}(\tfrac12)R2∼Exp(21​) is −2ln⁡u1-2\ln u_1−2lnu1​ by inverse transform (rate λ=12\lambda = \tfrac12λ=21​ gives −1λln⁡u=−2ln⁡u-\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln u = -2\ln u−λ1​lnu=−2lnu), and Θ=2πu2\Theta = 2\pi u_2Θ=2πu2​. Converting back from polar to Cartesian coordinates then yields two independent standard normals.

Algorithm (Box–Muller).

  1. Generate u1⊥u2∼U(0,1)u_1 \perp u_2 \sim U(0,1)u1​⊥u2​∼U(0,1).
  2. Return

X1=−2ln⁡u1 cos⁡(2πu2),X2=−2ln⁡u1 sin⁡(2πu2).X_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln u_1}\,\cos(2\pi u_2), \qquad X_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln u_1}\,\sin(2\pi u_2). X1​=−2lnu1​​cos(2πu2​),X2​=−2lnu1​​sin(2πu2​).

Two uniforms in, two independent N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) variates out — exact, no rejection.

Two cautions.

  • The uniforms must really be independent. If u1,u2u_1, u_2u1​,u2​ are consecutive outputs of a poor LCG (recall RANDU, §3.2.3), the pairs (u1,u2)(u_1, u_2)(u1​,u2​) lie on a few lines in the unit square, and after the transformation the points (X1,X2)(X_1, X_2)(X1​,X2​) fall on a visible spiral in the plane. In practice one uses separate streams for u1u_1u1​ and u2u_2u2​ (§3.3, practical issue 3).
  • Cost. One logarithm, one square root, one sine and one cosine per pair. The trigonometric functions are expensive, which motivates the next algorithm.

The polar method avoids sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos by generating the angle geometrically instead of computing it.

W=−2ln⁡SSW = \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln S}{S}} W=S−2lnS​​

cos⁡Θ=V1S,sin⁡Θ=V2S,and S itself is the uniform we need, so R=−2ln⁡S.\cos\Theta = \frac{V_1}{\sqrt S}, \qquad \sin\Theta = \frac{V_2}{\sqrt S}, \qquad \text{and } S \text{ itself is the uniform we need, so } R = \sqrt{-2\ln S}. cosΘ=S​V1​​,sinΘ=S​V2​​,and S itself is the uniform we need, so R=−2lnS​.

and likewise X2=V2WX_2 = V_2 WX2​=V2​W. The cosine and sine have been replaced by a division.

P(accept)=P(S≤1)=area of unit diskarea of square=π4≈0.785P(\text{accept}) = P(S \le 1) = \dfrac{\text{area of unit disk}}{\text{area of square}} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785P(accept)=P(S≤1)=area of squarearea of unit disk​=4π​≈0.785, so on average 4/π≈1.274/\pi \approx 1.274/π≈1.27 attempts, i.e. about 2.552.552.55 uniforms per pair of normals.   1. Generate Y∼N(μ,σ2)Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)Y∼N(μ,σ2).

4.3.4. Truncated distributions

Suppose we want XXX restricted to an interval [a,b][a, b][a,b]. There are two different things “truncate” can mean:

  • Redistribute the mass that falls outside [a,b][a,b][a,b] proportionally over [a,b][a,b][a,b] — the conditional distribution of XXX given a≤X≤ba \le X \le ba≤X≤b.
  • Pile up the outside mass at the endpoints: values below aaa become aaa, values above bbb become bbb. This is clipping, X∗=min⁡(max⁡(X,a),b)X^* = \min(\max(X, a), b)X∗=min(max(X,a),b), and it creates atoms at aaa and bbb.

The first is the usual meaning. Its c.d.f. is

F~(x)=F(x)−F(a)F(b)−F(a),a≤x≤b,\tilde F(x) = \frac{F(x) - F(a)}{F(b) - F(a)}, \qquad a \le x \le b, F~(x)=F(b)−F(a)F(x)−F(a)​,a≤x≤b,

with density f~(x)=f(x)F(b)−F(a)\tilde f(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{F(b) - F(a)}f~​(x)=F(b)−F(a)f(x)​ on [a,b][a,b][a,b] — the original density scaled up by the constant 1/(F(b)−F(a))1/(F(b)-F(a))1/(F(b)−F(a)) so that it integrates to 1 again. (Check: F~(x)=∫axf(y)F(b)−F(a) dy=F(x)−F(a)F(b)−F(a)\tilde F(x) = \int_a^x \frac{f(y)}{F(b)-F(a)}\,dy = \frac{F(x)-F(a)}{F(b)-F(a)}F~(x)=∫ax​F(b)−F(a)f(y)​dy=F(b)−F(a)F(x)−F(a)​.)

Inverting F~\tilde FF~ is one line:

u=F(x)−F(a)F(b)−F(a)  ⟹  F(x)=F(a)+u [F(b)−F(a)]  ⟹  x=F−1(F(a)+u [F(b)−F(a)]).u = \frac{F(x) - F(a)}{F(b) - F(a)} \;\Longrightarrow\; F(x) = F(a) + u\,[F(b) - F(a)] \;\Longrightarrow\; x = F^{-1}\big(F(a) + u\,[F(b)-F(a)]\big). u=F(b)−F(a)F(x)−F(a)​⟹F(x)=F(a)+u[F(b)−F(a)]⟹x=F−1(F(a)+u[F(b)−F(a)]).

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. Return X=F−1(F(a)+u [F(b)−F(a)])X = F^{-1}\big(F(a) + u\,[F(b) - F(a)]\big)X=F−1(F(a)+u[F(b)−F(a)]).

This is the “advantage 3” of §4.2.1 in detail. The alternative — generate from FFF and reject anything outside [a,b][a,b][a,b] — is acceptance–rejection with efficiency F(b)−F(a)F(b) - F(a)F(b)−F(a), which can be tiny if the interval is in a tail; the inverse-transform version uses every uniform.

  1. Generate uuu; let P=(n−1)uP = (n-1)uP=(n−1)u and I=⌊P⌋+1I = \lfloor P \rfloor + 1I=⌊P⌋+1.

The output always lies in [X(1),X(n)][X_{(1)}, X_{(n)}][X(1)​,X(n)​] — no values beyond the observed range can ever appear, which is the known limitation of empirical input modelling.

4.4. Generating Discrete Random Variates

Inverse transform works for every discrete distribution (§4.2.1), but is not always the fastest. Besides the specific formulas below, the section ends with two table-based methods — table lookup and the alias method — that trade setup and storage for speed.

Bernoulli(p)(p)(p). X=1X = 1X=1 with probability ppp, 000 with probability 1−p1-p1−p. Inverse transform with two values:

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. If u≤pu \le pu≤p, return X=1X = 1X=1; otherwise return X=0X = 0X=0.

Binomial(n,p)(n, p)(n,p). The number of successes in nnn independent Bernoulli(p)(p)(p) trials is a sum, so use convolution:

  1. Generate Y1,…,YnY_1, \dots, Y_nY1​,…,Yn​ i.i.d. Bernoulli(p)(p)(p).
  2. Return X=Y1+⋯+YnX = Y_1 + \cdots + Y_nX=Y1​+⋯+Yn​.

Costs nnn uniforms per variate; fine for small nnn.

Discrete uniform DU(i,j)DU(i, j)DU(i,j). P(X=k)=1j−i+1P(X = k) = \dfrac{1}{j-i+1}P(X=k)=j−i+11​ for k=i,i+1,…,jk = i, i+1, \dots, jk=i,i+1,…,j. Generalizing the ⌈100u⌉\lceil 100u \rceil⌈100u⌉ trick of §4.2.1:

Here ⌊x⌋\lfloor x \rfloor⌊x⌋ is the largest integer ≤x\le x≤x. The product (j−i+1)u(j-i+1)u(j−i+1)u is uniform on [0,j−i+1)[0, j-i+1)[0,j−i+1); its floor is uniform on {0,1,…,j−i}\{0, 1, \dots, j-i\}{0,1,…,j−i}; adding iii shifts to {i,…,j}\{i, \dots, j\}{i,…,j}. (The floor form is slightly safer than the ceiling form when uuu can be exactly 000.)

Geometric(p)(p)(p). p(k)=(1−p)k−1pp(k) = (1-p)^{k-1}pp(k)=(1−p)k−1p, k=1,2,…k = 1, 2, \dotsk=1,2,… — the number of trials up to and including the first success. Instead of simulating the trials (§4.2.5), invert the c.d.f. in closed form. The inverse-transform intervals are

0<u≤p⇒X=1,p<u≤p+(1−p)p⇒X=2,…0 < u \le p \Rightarrow X = 1, \qquad p < u \le p + (1-p)p \Rightarrow X = 2, \qquad \dots 0<u≤p⇒X=1,p<u≤p+(1−p)p⇒X=2,…

∑i=1k−1(1−p)i−1p  <  u  ≤  ∑i=1k(1−p)i−1p.\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}(1-p)^{i-1}p \;<\; u \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^{k}(1-p)^{i-1}p . i=1∑k−1​(1−p)i−1p<u≤i=1∑k​(1−p)i−1p.

Each side is a geometric series: ∑i=1k(1−p)i−1p=p 1−(1−p)k1−(1−p)=1−(1−p)k\sum_{i=1}^{k}(1-p)^{i-1}p = p\,\dfrac{1 - (1-p)^k}{1 - (1-p)} = 1 - (1-p)^k∑i=1k​(1−p)i−1p=p1−(1−p)1−(1−p)k​=1−(1−p)k. So the condition is

The formula is the discrete twin of the exponential’s −1λln⁡u-\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln u−λ1​lnu: the geometric is the exponential’s discrete analogue (it has the same memoryless property), and the generators have the same shape.

Arbitrary discrete distribution. X∈{0,1,…,n}X \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}X∈{0,1,…,n} with P(X=i)=p(i)P(X = i) = p(i)P(X=i)=p(i). Inverse transform:

4.4.1. Table lookup

Idea. If all probabilities are given to qqq decimal places, then each p(i)p(i)p(i) is a whole number of units of size 10−q10^{-q}10−q. Build a vector mmm of length 10q10^q10q in which value iii appears 10q p(i)10^q\,p(i)10qp(i) times. Picking a uniformly random entry of mmm then returns iii with exactly the right probability — no search at all.

Example. P(0)=0.15P(0) = 0.15P(0)=0.15, P(1)=0.20P(1) = 0.20P(1)=0.20, P(2)=0.37P(2) = 0.37P(2)=0.37, P(3)=0.28P(3) = 0.28P(3)=0.28, so q=2q = 2q=2. Construct mmm of length 100100100:

m=[0,…,0⏟15,  1,…,1⏟20,  2,…,2⏟37,  3,…,3⏟28].m = [\underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_{15},\; \underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_{20},\; \underbrace{2, \dots, 2}_{37},\; \underbrace{3, \dots, 3}_{28}] . m=[150,…,0​​,201,…,1​​,372,…,2​​,283,…,3​​].

  1. Generate J∼DU(1,100)J \sim DU(1, 100)J∼DU(1,100), i.e. J=1+⌊100u⌋J = 1 + \lfloor 100u \rfloorJ=1+⌊100u⌋.
  2. Return X=mJX = m_JX=mJ​.

Check: P(X=2)=P(J lands on one of the 37 entries equal to 2)=37/100P(X = 2) = P(J \text{ lands on one of the 37 entries equal to } 2) = 37/100P(X=2)=P(J lands on one of the 37 entries equal to 2)=37/100. ✓

Simple and very fast (one uniform, one index), but it needs setup and 10q10^q10q storage locations — q=6q = 6q=6 already means a million entries.

4.4.2. Improved table lookup

Idea. Split each probability by decimal digit and keep one table per digit. Same example:

iii p(i)p(i)p(i) tenths digit hundredths digit
0 0.15 1 5
1 0.20 2 0
2 0.37 3 7
3 0.28 2 8
sum 8 20

Build one table from the tenths digits (value iii appears “tenths digit” times) and one from the hundredths digits:

m(1)=[0, 1,1, 2,2,2, 3,3](length 8),m(2)=[0,…,0⏟5, 2,…,2⏟7, 3,…,3⏟8](length 20).m^{(1)} = [0,\ 1, 1,\ 2, 2, 2,\ 3, 3] \quad (\text{length } 8), \qquad m^{(2)} = [\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{5},\ \underbrace{2,\dots,2}_{7},\ \underbrace{3,\dots,3}_{8}] \quad (\text{length } 20). m(1)=[0, 1,1, 2,2,2, 3,3](length 8),m(2)=[50,…,0​​, 72,…,2​​, 83,…,3​​](length 20).

Total storage 8+20=288 + 20 = 288+20=28 instead of 100100100. (Value 1 is absent from m(2)m^{(2)}m(2) because its hundredths digit is 000.)

The tenths table carries total mass 8/10=0.88/10 = 0.88/10=0.8 and the hundredths table carries 20/100=0.220/100 = 0.220/100=0.2. So:

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. If u≤0.8u \le 0.8u≤0.8, generate J1∼DU(1,8)J_1 \sim DU(1, 8)J1​∼DU(1,8) and return X=mJ1(1)X = m^{(1)}_{J_1}X=mJ1​(1)​.
  3. Otherwise generate J2∼DU(1,20)J_2 \sim DU(1, 20)J2​∼DU(1,20) and return X=mJ2(2)X = m^{(2)}_{J_2}X=mJ2​(2)​.

Check: P(X=2)=P(X=2∣table 1) P(table 1)+P(X=2∣table 2) P(table 2)=38⋅810+720⋅210=0.30+0.07=0.37P(X = 2) = P(X = 2 \mid \text{table 1})\,P(\text{table 1}) + P(X = 2 \mid \text{table 2})\,P(\text{table 2}) = \frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{8}{10} + \frac{7}{20}\cdot\frac{2}{10} = 0.30 + 0.07 = 0.37P(X=2)=P(X=2∣table 1)P(table 1)+P(X=2∣table 2)P(table 2)=83​⋅108​+207​⋅102​=0.30+0.07=0.37. ✓ The two terms are exactly the tenths and hundredths parts of 0.370.370.37.

This is composition (§4.2.2) in disguise: p=0.8 p(1)+0.2 p(2)p = 0.8\,p^{(1)} + 0.2\,p^{(2)}p=0.8p(1)+0.2p(2), where p(j)p^{(j)}p(j) is the uniform-pick distribution on table jjj. It costs two uniforms per variate instead of one, in exchange for far less storage when qqq is large.

4.4.3. The alias method

The alias method keeps table lookup’s speed — one uniform-pick plus one comparison — with only 2(n+1)2(n+1)2(n+1) storage locations, whatever the precision of the probabilities.

Setup. Two vectors of length n+1n+1n+1:

  • cutoff values F0,F1,…,Fn∈[0,1]F_0, F_1, \dots, F_n \in [0,1]F0​,F1​,…,Fn​∈[0,1],
  • aliases L0,L1,…,Ln∈{0,1,…,n}L_0, L_1, \dots, L_n \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}L0​,L1​,…,Ln​∈{0,1,…,n}.

Algorithm.

  1. Generate I∼DU(0,n)I \sim DU(0, n)I∼DU(0,n) and u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1) independently.
  2. If u≤FIu \le F_Iu≤FI​, return X=IX = IX=I; otherwise return X=LIX = L_IX=LI​.

How to read it. Each value III is drawn with probability 1n+1\frac{1}{n+1}n+11​ — an equal-size “column”. Inside column III, a fraction FIF_IFI​ of the column belongs to III itself and the remaining 1−FI1 - F_I1−FI​ belongs to one other value, its alias LIL_ILI​. So

P(X=k)=1n+1[ Fk+∑i : Li=k(1−Fi)]:P(X = k) = \frac{1}{n+1}\Big[\,F_k + \sum_{i \,:\, L_i = k} (1 - F_i)\Big] : P(X=k)=n+11​[Fk​+i:Li​=k∑​(1−Fi​)]:

kkk’s own share of its column, plus whatever the other columns hand to it as an alias. The setup consists of choosing FFF and LLL so that this equals p(k)p(k)p(k) for every kkk.

It resembles acceptance–rejection (draw a candidate, compare uuu to a threshold), with one crucial difference: on “rejection” we do not start over — we return the alias. There is no loop, so exactly one III and one uuu are consumed per variate.

Scale by n+1n+1n+1: q=4p=(0.60,0.80,1.48,1.12)q = 4p = (0.60, 0.80, 1.48, 1.12)q=4p=(0.60,0.80,1.48,1.12). 4.5. Generating Random Vectors

Why a separate section. Everything so far produces one random variable at a time, and successive variates are independent. Many inputs come in correlated groups: a job’s processing times at two consecutive stations, a customer’s order size and service time, daily demands for related products. Generating each coordinate on its own throws the correlation away. We need a way to produce a whole vector X=(X1,…,Xd)TX = (X_1, \dots, X_d)^{\mathsf T}X=(X1​,…,Xd​)T with a prescribed mean and a prescribed dependence structure.

4.5.1. Mean vector and covariance matrix

For a random vector X∈RdX \in \mathbb{R}^dX∈Rd:

μ=E[X]=(E[X1],…,E[Xd])T,Σ=cov⁡(X)=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)T],\mu = \mathbf{E}[X] = \big(\mathbf{E}[X_1], \dots, \mathbf{E}[X_d]\big)^{\mathsf T}, \qquad \Sigma = \operatorname{cov}(X) = \mathbf{E}\big[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\big], μ=E[X]=(E[X1​],…,E[Xd​])T,Σ=cov(X)=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)T],

so Σ\SigmaΣ is d×dd \times dd×d with entries Σij=cov⁡(Xi,Xj)\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{cov}(X_i, X_j)Σij​=cov(Xi​,Xj​) — variances on the diagonal, covariances off it (§2.3). Two facts about Σ\SigmaΣ that the construction below relies on:

  • Σ\SigmaΣ is symmetric, since cov⁡(Xi,Xj)=cov⁡(Xj,Xi)\operatorname{cov}(X_i, X_j) = \operatorname{cov}(X_j, X_i)cov(Xi​,Xj​)=cov(Xj​,Xi​).
  • Σ\SigmaΣ is positive semidefinite: for any constant vector aaa, aTΣa=Var⁡(aTX)≥0a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a = \operatorname{Var}(a^{\mathsf T}X) \ge 0aTΣa=Var(aTX)≥0. A variance cannot be negative.

Linear transformations. If Y=b+AXY = b + AXY=b+AX for a constant vector bbb and constant matrix AAA, then

E[Y]=b+Aμ,cov⁡(Y)=A Σ AT.\mathbf{E}[Y] = b + A\mu, \qquad \operatorname{cov}(Y) = A\,\Sigma\,A^{\mathsf T}. E[Y]=b+Aμ,cov(Y)=AΣAT.

(The second follows from Y−E[Y]=A(X−μ)Y - \mathbf{E}[Y] = A(X - \mu)Y−E[Y]=A(X−μ), so cov⁡(Y)=E[A(X−μ)(X−μ)TAT]=AΣAT\operatorname{cov}(Y) = \mathbf{E}[A(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}] = A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}cov(Y)=E[A(X−μ)(X−μ)TAT]=AΣAT.) This is the whole trick: we can manufacture any covariance we like by applying a matrix to something simple.

4.5.2. The multivariate normal distribution

X∼Nd(μ,Σ)X \sim N_d(\mu, \Sigma)X∼Nd​(μ,Σ) is the ddd-dimensional normal with mean vector μ\muμ and covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ. Its one property we need: a linear transformation of a multivariate normal is again multivariate normal. Combined with the formulas above, if X∼Nd(μ,Σ)X \sim N_d(\mu, \Sigma)X∼Nd​(μ,Σ) then b+AX∼N(b+Aμ,  AΣAT)b + AX \sim N(b + A\mu,\; A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T})b+AX∼N(b+Aμ,AΣAT).

The simplest member of the family is the standard one. Let Z1,…,ZdZ_1, \dots, Z_dZ1​,…,Zd​ be i.i.d. N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) (§4.3.1) and Z=(Z1,…,Zd)TZ = (Z_1, \dots, Z_d)^{\mathsf T}Z=(Z1​,…,Zd​)T. Then E[Z]=0\mathbf{E}[Z] = 0E[Z]=0 and cov⁡(Z)=Id\operatorname{cov}(Z) = I_dcov(Z)=Id​ (variances 1, covariances 0 by independence), so Z∼Nd(0,Id)Z \sim N_d(0, I_d)Z∼Nd​(0,Id​).

The plan. Take X=μ+AZX = \mu + AZX=μ+AZ. Then XXX is multivariate normal with

E[X]=μ,cov⁡(X)=A I AT=AAT.\mathbf{E}[X] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{cov}(X) = A\,I\,A^{\mathsf T} = AA^{\mathsf T}. E[X]=μ,cov(X)=AIAT=AAT.

So all we need is a matrix AAA with

AAT=Σ,AA^{\mathsf T} = \Sigma, AAT=Σ,

a “square root” of Σ\SigmaΣ. There are two standard ways to get one; the lecture uses the second.

  1. Cholesky factorization. Any symmetric positive-definite Σ\SigmaΣ can be written Σ=LLT\Sigma = LL^{\mathsf T}Σ=LLT with LLL lower-triangular. Take A=LA = LA=L. Cheap to compute (O(d3/3)O(d^3/3)O(d3/3)) and what most software does.
  2. Eigenvalue (spectral) decomposition — next.

4.5.3. Eigenvalue decomposition

Definitions. For a d×dd \times dd×d matrix Σ\SigmaΣ, if a constant λ\lambdaλ and a non-zero vector vvv satisfy

Σv=λv,\Sigma v = \lambda v, Σv=λv,

then λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of Σ\SigmaΣ and vvv a corresponding eigenvector. (Geometrically: Σ\SigmaΣ merely stretches vvv by the factor λ\lambdaλ without turning it.)

Facts for a real symmetric matrix (spectral theorem):

  • It has ddd linearly independent eigenvectors, which can be chosen orthogonal and of unit length: v1,…,vdv_1, \dots, v_dv1​,…,vd​ with viTvj=0v_i^{\mathsf T}v_j = 0viT​vj​=0 for i≠ji \ne ji=j and ∥vi∥=1\|v_i\| = 1∥vi​∥=1.
  • Put them side by side in P=[v1  v2  ⋯  vd]P = [v_1 \; v_2 \; \cdots \; v_d]P=[v1​v2​⋯vd​]. Orthonormal columns mean PTP=IP^{\mathsf T}P = IPTP=I, i.e. P−1=PTP^{-1} = P^{\mathsf T}P−1=PT — the inverse is free.
  • With Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λd)\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d)Λ=diag(λ1​,…,λd​),

Σ=P Λ PT.\Sigma = P\,\Lambda\,P^{\mathsf T}. Σ=PΛPT.

  • Because Σ\SigmaΣ is positive semidefinite, every λi≥0\lambda_i \ge 0λi​≥0 (λi=viTΣvi≥0\lambda_i = v_i^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v_i \ge 0λi​=viT​Σvi​≥0), so Λ1/2=diag⁡(λ1,…,λd)\Lambda^{1/2} = \operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \dots, \sqrt{\lambda_d})Λ1/2=diag(λ1​​,…,λd​​) is a real matrix with Λ1/2Λ1/2=Λ\Lambda^{1/2}\Lambda^{1/2} = \LambdaΛ1/2Λ1/2=Λ.

The square root. Take A=PΛ1/2A = P\Lambda^{1/2}A=PΛ1/2. Then

AAT=PΛ1/2 (PΛ1/2)T=PΛ1/2Λ1/2PT=PΛPT=Σ.  ✓AA^{\mathsf T} = P\Lambda^{1/2}\,(P\Lambda^{1/2})^{\mathsf T} = P\Lambda^{1/2}\Lambda^{1/2}P^{\mathsf T} = P\Lambda P^{\mathsf T} = \Sigma. \; \checkmark AAT=PΛ1/2(PΛ1/2)T=PΛ1/2Λ1/2PT=PΛPT=Σ.✓

(We used (Λ1/2)T=Λ1/2(\Lambda^{1/2})^{\mathsf T} = \Lambda^{1/2}(Λ1/2)T=Λ1/2 since it is diagonal.)

Verification, step by step. Let Z=(Z1,…,Zd)TZ = (Z_1, \dots, Z_d)^{\mathsf T}Z=(Z1​,…,Zd​)T with ZiZ_iZi​ i.i.d. N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) and define

X=μ+PΛ1/2Z.X = \mu + P\Lambda^{1/2}Z . X=μ+PΛ1/2Z.

Mean: E[X]=μ+PΛ1/2 E[Z]=μ+0=μ\mathbf{E}[X] = \mu + P\Lambda^{1/2}\,\mathbf{E}[Z] = \mu + 0 = \muE[X]=μ+PΛ1/2E[Z]=μ+0=μ.

Covariance:

cov⁡(X)=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)T]=E[PΛ1/2Z ZTΛ1/2PT](X−μ=PΛ1/2Z; (ABC)T=CTBTAT)=PΛ1/2 E[ZZT] Λ1/2PT(constants come out of the expectation)=PΛ1/2 I Λ1/2PT(E[ZiZj]=1 if i=j, 0 otherwise)=PΛPT=Σ.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{cov}(X) &= \mathbf{E}\big[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\big] \\ &= \mathbf{E}\big[P\Lambda^{1/2}Z\,Z^{\mathsf T}\Lambda^{1/2}P^{\mathsf T}\big] && (X-\mu = P\Lambda^{1/2}Z;\ (ABC)^{\mathsf T} = C^{\mathsf T}B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}) \\ &= P\Lambda^{1/2}\,\mathbf{E}[ZZ^{\mathsf T}]\,\Lambda^{1/2}P^{\mathsf T} && (\text{constants come out of the expectation}) \\ &= P\Lambda^{1/2}\,I\,\Lambda^{1/2}P^{\mathsf T} && (\mathbf{E}[Z_iZ_j] = 1 \text{ if } i=j,\ 0 \text{ otherwise}) \\ &= P\Lambda P^{\mathsf T} = \Sigma . \end{aligned} cov(X)​=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)T]=E[PΛ1/2ZZTΛ1/2PT]=PΛ1/2E[ZZT]Λ1/2PT=PΛ1/2IΛ1/2PT=PΛPT=Σ.​​(X−μ=PΛ1/2Z; (ABC)T=CTBTAT)(constants come out of the expectation)(E[Zi​Zj​]=1 if i=j, 0 otherwise)​

And XXX is normal because each coordinate is a linear combination of the independent normals Z1,…,ZdZ_1, \dots, Z_dZ1​,…,Zd​ plus a constant.

Algorithm (multivariate normal via eigen decomposition).

Setup (once): compute the eigenvalues λi\lambda_iλi​ and orthonormal eigenvectors viv_ivi​ of Σ\SigmaΣ; form PPP and Λ1/2\Lambda^{1/2}Λ1/2; store A=PΛ1/2A = P\Lambda^{1/2}A=PΛ1/2.

  1. Generate Z1,…,ZdZ_1, \dots, Z_dZ1​,…,Zd​ i.i.d. N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) (Box–Muller or polar method, §4.3).

One matrix–vector multiplication per vector; the expensive part (the decomposition) is paid once.

Example (d=2d = 2d=2). Two correlated standard normals with correlation ρ\rhoρ:

μ=(μ1μ2),Σ=(1ρρ1).\mu = \begin{pmatrix}\mu_1\\ \mu_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}. μ=(μ1​μ2​​),Σ=(1ρ​ρ1​).

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors (check by multiplying out):

Σ(11)=(1+ρ)(11),Σ(1−1)=(1−ρ)(1−1),\Sigma\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = (1+\rho)\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} = (1-\rho)\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}, Σ(11​)=(1+ρ)(11​),Σ(1−1​)=(1−ρ)(1−1​),

so λ1=1+ρ\lambda_1 = 1+\rhoλ1​=1+ρ, λ2=1−ρ\lambda_2 = 1-\rhoλ2​=1−ρ (both ≥0\ge 0≥0 since ∣ρ∣≤1|\rho| \le 1∣ρ∣≤1), and after normalizing to unit length,

P=12(111−1),Λ1/2=(1+ρ001−ρ),A=PΛ1/2=12(1+ρ1−ρ1+ρ−1−ρ).P = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda^{1/2} = \begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1+\rho} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{1-\rho}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A = P\Lambda^{1/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{1+\rho} & \sqrt{1-\rho} \\ \sqrt{1+\rho} & -\sqrt{1-\rho}\end{pmatrix}. P=2​1​(11​1−1​),Λ1/2=(1+ρ​0​01−ρ​​),A=PΛ1/2=2​1​(1+ρ​1+ρ​​1−ρ​−1−ρ​​).

The algorithm therefore returns

X1=μ1+1+ρ Z1+1−ρ Z22,X2=μ2+1+ρ Z1−1−ρ Z22.X_1 = \mu_1 + \frac{\sqrt{1+\rho}\,Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,Z_2}{\sqrt2}, \qquad X_2 = \mu_2 + \frac{\sqrt{1+\rho}\,Z_1 - \sqrt{1-\rho}\,Z_2}{\sqrt2}. X1​=μ1​+2​1+ρ​Z1​+1−ρ​Z2​​,X2​=μ2​+2​1+ρ​Z1​−1−ρ​Z2​​.

Check: Var⁡(X1)=(1+ρ)+(1−ρ)2=1\operatorname{Var}(X_1) = \frac{(1+\rho) + (1-\rho)}{2} = 1Var(X1​)=2(1+ρ)+(1−ρ)​=1, and cov⁡(X1,X2)=(1+ρ)−(1−ρ)2=ρ\operatorname{cov}(X_1, X_2) = \frac{(1+\rho) - (1-\rho)}{2} = \rhocov(X1​,X2​)=2(1+ρ)−(1−ρ)​=ρ. ✓

The same Σ\SigmaΣ by Cholesky. L=(10ρ1−ρ2)L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \rho & \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\end{pmatrix}L=(1ρ​01−ρ2​​) satisfies LLT=ΣLL^{\mathsf T} = \SigmaLLT=Σ, giving

X1=μ1+Z1,X2=μ2+ρZ1+1−ρ2 Z2.X_1 = \mu_1 + Z_1, \qquad X_2 = \mu_2 + \rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z_2 . X1​=μ1​+Z1​,X2​=μ2​+ρZ1​+1−ρ2​Z2​.

Different formulas, same distribution — both are valid square roots of Σ\SigmaΣ. (For general variances σ12,σ22\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2σ12​,σ22​: X1=μ1+σ1Z1X_1 = \mu_1 + \sigma_1 Z_1X1​=μ1​+σ1​Z1​, X2=μ2+σ2(ρZ1+1−ρ2 Z2)X_2 = \mu_2 + \sigma_2(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z_2)X2​=μ2​+σ2​(ρZ1​+1−ρ2​Z2​).) The Cholesky form shows the mechanism plainly: X2X_2X2​ borrows a share ρ\rhoρ of X1X_1X1​’s noise and tops up with fresh noise so that its variance is still 1.

Remarks.

  • The ZiZ_iZi​ must be independent — this is where the quality of the normal generator (§4.3.1’s spiral warning) matters doubly.
  • The construction only controls the first two moments. For a non-normal vector with prescribed marginals and correlation, transforming ZZZ by a matrix destroys the marginals; one then uses ZZZ only to carry the dependence and maps each coordinate through Fi−1(Φ(⋅))F_i^{-1}(\Phi(\cdot))Fi−1​(Φ(⋅)) (the “NORTA” idea). Beyond the scope of this course.

4.6. Generating Stochastic Processes

A stochastic process (§2.5) is a whole family of random variables indexed by time. Generating one means generating a sample path. The workhorse is the Poisson process — the arrival process of almost every queueing model — and its time-varying generalization.

4.6.1. The Poisson process

Counting process. Let SnS_nSn​ be the time of the nnn-th event (the nnn-th arrival time), with S0=0S_0 = 0S0​=0, and let

Xn=Sn−Sn−1X_n = S_n - S_{n-1} Xn​=Sn​−Sn−1​

be the nnn-th interarrival time, so Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​. Define

N(t)=max⁡{n:Sn≤t}=number of events that have occurred up to time t.N(t) = \max\{n : S_n \le t\} = \text{number of events that have occurred up to time } t . N(t)=max{n:Sn​≤t}=number of events that have occurred up to time t.

{N(t):t≥0}\{N(t) : t \ge 0\}{N(t):t≥0} is a counting process: it starts at 000, is integer-valued, non-decreasing, and jumps by 111 at each SnS_nSn​.

Definition. If the interarrival times X1,X2,…X_1, X_2, \dotsX1​,X2​,… are i.i.d. Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ), then {N(t)}\{N(t)\}{N(t)} is called a Poisson process with rate λ\lambdaλ, written PP(λ)\text{PP}(\lambda)PP(λ).

Properties of PP(λ)\text{PP}(\lambda)PP(λ).

  1. Poisson counts. For every ttt,

    P(N(t)=k)=e−λt(λt)kk!,k=0,1,2,…,P(N(t) = k) = e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(\lambda t)^k}{k!}, \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, P(N(t)=k)=e−λtk!(λt)k​,k=0,1,2,…,

    i.e. N(t)∼Poisson(λt)N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)N(t)∼Poisson(λt), so E[N(t)]=λt\mathbf{E}[N(t)] = \lambda tE[N(t)]=λt. Hence λ=E[N(t)]/t\lambda = \mathbf{E}[N(t)]/tλ=E[N(t)]/t: the rate (or arrival rate) is the expected number of events per unit time. More generally the number of events in any interval of length sss is Poisson(λs)\text{Poisson}(\lambda s)Poisson(λs), and counts in disjoint intervals are independent. (This is the Erlang formula of §4.2.3 read the other way: P(N(t)≥n)=P(Sn≤t)P(N(t) \ge n) = P(S_n \le t)P(N(t)≥n)=P(Sn​≤t).)

  2. Arrival-time theorem. Given that N(t)=kN(t) = kN(t)=k, the kkk arrival times (S1,…,Sk)(S_1, \dots, S_k)(S1​,…,Sk​) are distributed as the order statistics of kkk i.i.d. U(0,t)U(0, t)U(0,t) random variables. That is: take U1,…,UkU_1, \dots, U_kU1​,…,Uk​ i.i.d. U(0,t)U(0,t)U(0,t), sort them into ascending order Uˉ(1)<Uˉ(2)<⋯<Uˉ(k)\bar U_{(1)} < \bar U_{(2)} < \cdots < \bar U_{(k)}Uˉ(1)​<Uˉ(2)​<⋯<Uˉ(k)​; then (S1,…,Sk)(S_1, \dots, S_k)(S1​,…,Sk​) has the same joint distribution as (Uˉ(1),…,Uˉ(k))(\bar U_{(1)}, \dots, \bar U_{(k)})(Uˉ(1)​,…,Uˉ(k)​). In words: given how many events occurred, they are scattered uniformly and independently over the interval — the Poisson process has no preferred times.

Bernoulli splitting. Let {N(t)}\{N(t)\}{N(t)} be PP(λ)\text{PP}(\lambda)PP(λ) and fix probabilities p1,…,pr>0p_1, \dots, p_r > 0p1​,…,pr​>0 with ∑j=1rpj=1\sum_{j=1}^r p_j = 1∑j=1r​pj​=1. Assign each arrival, independently of everything else, to category iii with probability pip_ipi​, and let Ni(t)N_i(t)Ni​(t) count the category-iii arrivals, so N(t)=N1(t)+⋯+Nr(t)N(t) = N_1(t) + \cdots + N_r(t)N(t)=N1​(t)+⋯+Nr​(t).

Theorem. Under Bernoulli splitting the rrr processes {N1(t)},…,{Nr(t)}\{N_1(t)\}, \dots, \{N_r(t)\}{N1​(t)},…,{Nr​(t)} are independent Poisson processes, with {Ni(t)}∼PP(λpi)\{N_i(t)\} \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p_i){Ni​(t)}∼PP(λpi​).

The case r=2r = 2r=2, with probabilities ppp and 1−p1-p1−p, is the one we will use: the arrivals that pass a coin toss form PP(λp)\text{PP}(\lambda p)PP(λp), those that fail form PP(λ(1−p))\text{PP}(\lambda(1-p))PP(λ(1−p)), and the two streams are independent of each other. (The independence is the surprising part: knowing many arrivals went to stream 1 tells you nothing about stream 2.)

4.6.2. The nonhomogeneous Poisson process

Motivation: traffic on a highway. A PP(λ)\text{PP}(\lambda)PP(λ) has one constant rate for all time. Real arrival rates vary:

A single λ\lambdaλ would average the rush hours and the quiet hours together and get both wrong. We need a process whose rate is a function of time.

Definition. A counting process {N(t)}\{N(t)\}{N(t)} is a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NPP) with rate function λ(t)≥0\lambda(t) \ge 0λ(t)≥0 if

  1. N(0)=0N(0) = 0N(0)=0;
  2. {N(t)}\{N(t)\}{N(t)} has independent increments: counts in disjoint time intervals are independent;
  3. in a short window (t,t+h](t, t+h](t,t+h],

    P(N(t+h)=k∣N(t)=k)=1−λ(t)h+o(h)(no event)P(N(t+h)=k+1∣N(t)=k)=λ(t)h+o(h)(exactly one event)P(N(t+h)=k+j∣N(t)=k)=o(h),j≥2(two or more events)\begin{aligned} P\big(N(t+h) = k \mid N(t) = k\big) &= 1 - \lambda(t)h + o(h) && \text{(no event)} \\ P\big(N(t+h) = k+1 \mid N(t) = k\big) &= \lambda(t)h + o(h) && \text{(exactly one event)} \\ P\big(N(t+h) = k+j \mid N(t) = k\big) &= o(h), \quad j \ge 2 && \text{(two or more events)} \end{aligned} P(N(t+h)=k∣N(t)=k)P(N(t+h)=k+1∣N(t)=k)P(N(t+h)=k+j∣N(t)=k)​=1−λ(t)h+o(h)=λ(t)h+o(h)=o(h),j≥2​​(no event)(exactly one event)(two or more events)​

    Here o(h)o(h)o(h) means a quantity that vanishes faster than hhh as h→0h \to 0h→0. In words: over a very short interval almost surely either 000 or 111 event happens, and the chance of 111 event is proportional to the length of the interval with proportionality constant λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t) — the current value of the rate.

Counts. Define the mean-value function m(t)=∫0tλ(s) dsm(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(s)\,dsm(t)=∫0t​λ(s)ds. Then

P(N(t)=k)=e−m(t)m(t)kk!,k=0,1,2,…,P(N(t) = k) = e^{-m(t)}\frac{m(t)^k}{k!}, \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, P(N(t)=k)=e−m(t)k!m(t)k​,k=0,1,2,…,

so N(t)∼Poisson(m(t))N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}\big(m(t)\big)N(t)∼Poisson(m(t)) and E[N(t)]=∫0tλ(s) ds\mathbf{E}[N(t)] = \int_0^t \lambda(s)\,dsE[N(t)]=∫0t​λ(s)ds — the area under the rate curve. More generally N(t+s)−N(t)∼Poisson(∫tt+sλ(u) du)N(t+s) - N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}\big(\int_t^{t+s}\lambda(u)\,du\big)N(t+s)−N(t)∼Poisson(∫tt+s​λ(u)du). With a constant rate λ(t)≡λ\lambda(t) \equiv \lambdaλ(t)≡λ we get m(t)=λtm(t) = \lambda tm(t)=λt and recover PP(λ)\text{PP}(\lambda)PP(λ): the NPP is the generalization.

Nonhomogeneous Bernoulli splitting. Now let the coin be biased by time: fix a function p(t):[0,∞)→[0,1]p(t) : [0, \infty) \to [0,1]p(t):[0,∞)→[0,1] and assign an arrival occurring at time ttt to stream 1 with probability p(t)p(t)p(t), to stream 2 with probability 1−p(t)1 - p(t)1−p(t).

Theorem. If {N(t)}∼PP(λ)\{N(t)\} \sim \text{PP}(\lambda){N(t)}∼PP(λ) is split with time-dependent probability p(t)p(t)p(t), then {N1(t)}\{N_1(t)\}{N1​(t)} and {N2(t)}\{N_2(t)\}{N2​(t)} are independent nonhomogeneous Poisson processes with rate functions λ p(t)\lambda\,p(t)λp(t) and λ (1−p(t))\lambda\,(1 - p(t))λ(1−p(t)):

P(N1(t)=k)=exp⁡ ⁣(−λ ⁣∫0tp(s) ds)[λ∫0tp(s) ds]kk!,P(N2(t)=k)=exp⁡ ⁣(−λ ⁣∫0t(1−p(s)) ds)[λ∫0t(1−p(s)) ds]kk!.P(N_1(t) = k) = \exp\!\Big(-\lambda\!\int_0^t p(s)\,ds\Big)\frac{\big[\lambda\int_0^t p(s)\,ds\big]^k}{k!}, \qquad P(N_2(t) = k) = \exp\!\Big(-\lambda\!\int_0^t (1-p(s))\,ds\Big)\frac{\big[\lambda\int_0^t (1-p(s))\,ds\big]^k}{k!}. P(N1​(t)=k)=exp(−λ∫0t​p(s)ds)k![λ∫0t​p(s)ds]k​,P(N2​(t)=k)=exp(−λ∫0t​(1−p(s))ds)k![λ∫0t​(1−p(s))ds]k​.

(The same holds if the parent process is itself an NPP with rate λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t): the pieces are NPPs with rates λ(t)p(t)\lambda(t)p(t)λ(t)p(t) and λ(t)(1−p(t))\lambda(t)(1-p(t))λ(t)(1−p(t)).) Thinning out a Poisson stream with a time-varying coin produces exactly an NPP — this is the key to generating one.

4.6.3. Generating a Poisson process on [0,T][0, T][0,T]

Approach 1: lay down the interarrival times. Since the gaps are i.i.d. Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ), generate them one at a time by inverse transform and accumulate. Set s0=0s_0 = 0s0​=0, i=0i = 0i=0.

  1. Generate u∼U(0,1)u \sim U(0,1)u∼U(0,1).
  2. Set si+1=si−1λln⁡us_{i+1} = s_i - \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln usi+1​=si​−λ1​lnu \quad(previous arrival plus an Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ) gap).
  3. Set i=i+1i = i + 1i=i+1.
  4. If si≤Ts_i \le Tsi​≤T, go back to step 1; otherwise stop. The arrival times are s1,…,si−1s_1, \dots, s_{i-1}s1​,…,si−1​ and N(T)=i−1N(T) = i - 1N(T)=i−1.

The last generated time, the one that overshoots TTT, is discarded; it only serves to tell us we are done. This is the natural method inside a discrete-event simulation, where the next arrival is scheduled as soon as the current one occurs.

Approach 2: use the arrival-time theorem. Decide the count first, then place the points.

  1. Generate N(T)∼Poisson(λT)N(T) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda T)N(T)∼Poisson(λT) (a discrete variate — inverse transform with the p.m.f. computed recursively, p(k+1)=p(k)⋅λT/(k+1)p(k+1) = p(k)\cdot\lambda T/(k+1)p(k+1)=p(k)⋅λT/(k+1)).
  2. Generate u1,…,uN(T)u_1, \dots, u_{N(T)}u1​,…,uN(T)​ i.i.d. U(0,T)U(0, T)U(0,T).
  3. Sort them; return uˉ(1)<uˉ(2)<⋯<uˉ(N(T))\bar u_{(1)} < \bar u_{(2)} < \cdots < \bar u_{(N(T))}uˉ(1)​<uˉ(2)​<⋯<uˉ(N(T))​ as the arrival times s1,…,sN(T)s_1, \dots, s_{N(T)}s1​,…,sN(T)​.

By property 2 the output has exactly the distribution of a PP(λ)\text{PP}(\lambda)PP(λ) path on [0,T][0,T][0,T]. This approach generates the whole path at once (convenient for vectorized code) at the cost of a sort.

4.6.4. Generating a nonhomogeneous Poisson process

A tempting but wrong method. Mimic Approach 1 with the current rate: having generated ti−1t_{i-1}ti−1​, draw the next gap from Exp(λ(ti−1))\text{Exp}(\lambda(t_{i-1}))Exp(λ(ti−1​)),

ti=ti−1−1λ(ti−1)ln⁡u.t_i = t_{i-1} - \frac{1}{\lambda(t_{i-1})}\ln u . ti​=ti−1​−λ(ti−1​)1​lnu.

This uses the rate at the previous arrival for the entire gap, as if the rate stayed frozen until the next event. It does not: the rate may rise steeply right after ti−1t_{i-1}ti−1​.

If λ(ti−1)\lambda(t_{i-1})λ(ti−1​) happens to be small, the gap has mean 1/λ(ti−1)1/\lambda(t_{i-1})1/λ(ti−1​), which is large, and the process can jump clean over a high-rate period in which many arrivals should have occurred. In a test with a rate function that dips to 0.250.250.25 and then peaks at 3.253.253.25, this method produced on average 3.93.93.9 arrivals on [0,10][0,10][0,10] where the true mean is 7.37.37.3, and only 1.51.51.5 arrivals in the rush-hour window where there should be 4.94.94.9. So this is not a correct way.

The correct way: the thinning method. Generate too many candidate arrivals from a homogeneous Poisson process whose rate is at least as large as λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t) everywhere, then keep each candidate at time ttt with probability λ(t)/λ∗\lambda(t)/\lambda^*λ(t)/λ∗. Let

λ∗=max⁡0≤t≤Tλ(t).\lambda^* = \max_{0 \le t \le T}\lambda(t). λ∗=0≤t≤Tmax​λ(t).

Algorithm (thinning), to generate tit_iti​ given ti−1t_{i-1}ti−1​:

  1. Set t=ti−1t = t_{i-1}t=ti−1​.
  2. Generate u1⊥u2∼U(0,1)u_1 \perp u_2 \sim U(0,1)u1​⊥u2​∼U(0,1).
  3. Set t=t−1λ∗ln⁡u1t = t - \dfrac{1}{\lambda^*}\ln u_1t=t−λ∗1​lnu1​ \quad(advance by an Exp(λ∗)\text{Exp}(\lambda^*)Exp(λ∗) gap: the next candidate).
  4. If u2≤λ(t)λ∗u_2 \le \dfrac{\lambda(t)}{\lambda^*}u2​≤λ∗λ(t)​, accept: set ti=tt_i = tti​=t. Otherwise go back to step 2 and try again (keeping the advanced ttt).

Repeat until t>Tt > Tt>T.

How to understand the algorithm. It is nonhomogeneous Bernoulli splitting run deliberately. The candidate times produced by steps 2–3 form a homogeneous PP(λ∗)\text{PP}(\lambda^*)PP(λ∗) — that is just Approach 1 with rate λ∗\lambda^*λ∗. Step 4 then assigns each candidate at time ttt to one of two streams with a time-dependent coin:

N1(t)=number of candidates accepted by time t,N2(t)=number rejected,p(t)=λ(t)λ∗.N_1(t) = \text{number of candidates accepted by time } t, \qquad N_2(t) = \text{number rejected}, \qquad p(t) = \frac{\lambda(t)}{\lambda^*}. N1​(t)=number of candidates accepted by time t,N2​(t)=number rejected,p(t)=λ∗λ(t)​.

By the splitting theorem, {N1(t)}\{N_1(t)\}{N1​(t)} is a nonhomogeneous Poisson process with rate function

λ∗⋅p(t)=λ∗⋅λ(t)λ∗=λ(t),\lambda^*\cdot p(t) = \lambda^*\cdot\frac{\lambda(t)}{\lambda^*} = \lambda(t), λ∗⋅p(t)=λ∗⋅λ∗λ(t)​=λ(t),

exactly the target. (The rejected stream is an NPP with rate λ∗−λ(t)\lambda^* - \lambda(t)λ∗−λ(t), independent of the accepted one — we simply throw it away.) Note that p(t)≤1p(t) \le 1p(t)≤1 precisely because λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ was chosen as the maximum of λ\lambdaλ; that is the only role λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ plays. The analogy with acceptance–rejection (§4.2.4) is exact: λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ is a flat majorizing function for λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t), and λ(t)/λ∗\lambda(t)/\lambda^*λ(t)/λ∗ is the acceptance probability.

Checks. In the same test as above, thinning gave 7.297.297.29 arrivals on average against the true 7.327.327.32, and 4.894.894.89 in the rush-hour window against 4.884.884.88.

Efficiency. The expected fraction of candidates accepted is

∫0Tλ(t) dtλ∗T=area under λarea of the rectangle,\frac{\int_0^T \lambda(t)\,dt}{\lambda^* T} = \frac{\text{area under } \lambda}{\text{area of the rectangle}}, λ∗T∫0T​λ(t)dt​=area of the rectanglearea under λ​,

the same picture as the AR efficiency 1/c1/c1/c. If λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t) has a sharp peak, λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ is large and most candidates are rejected during the quiet periods. The standard fix is the AR fix: use a piecewise constant λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ — split [0,T][0,T][0,T] into subintervals, each with its own local maximum — so the majorizing rectangle hugs the curve.

4.7.5. When each input is generated during the simulation

  • Demand at time ttt: generate the size DDD and set I←I−DI \leftarrow I - DI←I−D; generate the next interdemand time XXX and schedule the next demand at t+Xt + Xt+X.
  • Inventory evaluation (beginning of each month): if I<sI < sI<s, order Z=S−IZ = S - IZ=S−I, generate the lead time LLL, and schedule the order arrival at t+Lt + Lt+L. If I≥sI \ge sI≥s, nothing is generated.
  • Order arrival and end of simulation: no random input.
  • At t=0t = 0t=0, generate the first interdemand time to schedule the first demand.

4.7.6. Use a separate stream for each input

Following §3.3 (practical issue 3), take interdemand times, demand sizes and lead times from three different streams. The reason is concrete here: how many lead times are consumed depends on the policy (s,S)(s, S)(s,S), since a policy that orders more often uses more of them. With one shared stream, those extra draws would shift every later demand, and two policies would face different demand sequences. With separate streams, every (s,S)(s, S)(s,S) pair sees exactly the same demands (common random numbers, §4.2.1 advantage 4), so the difference in average cost reflects the policies rather than luck.
